title: Smallest Starting Charge for Every Chore
statement:
A robot must do every chore in chores, once each, in any order you choose. Chore i is [use, need]: the robot may only start it while its battery holds at least need, and finishing it drains use from the battery. Always use ≤ need.

The battery is never recharged. Return the smallest starting charge that lets the robot finish all chores.

examples.why: Start with 9: do [4, 9] (9 → 5), then [1, 5] (5 → 4), then [2, 3] (4 → 2). The chores only use 7, but [4, 9] needs 9 just to start.
Each chore uses all it needs, so the total use is the answer.
Sorting by need would start with [6, 8] and require 13. Doing [1, 7] first needs 9: 9 → 8, then 8 ≥ 8.

hints: The charge needed for a fixed order is easy to compute. Which order is best? Try two chores and compare both orders.
For two chores a and b, doing a first needs max(need_a, use_a + need_b). Work out when that beats the other order. The quantity need − use (the 'slack' a chore leaves unused) decides it.
Do chores with the largest need − use first. To compute the charge, walk that order backwards: charge = max(charge + use, need).

explain.intuition:
Each chore asks for need but only spends use; the gap need − use is charge that must be present but stays in the battery. A chore with a big gap is a good one to do early, while the battery is full anyway, because the unspent part then keeps serving the later chores. A chore whose need equals its use wastes nothing and can go last.

The exchange argument: for neighbors a then b, the pair needs max(need_a, use_a + need_b). Swapping them helps exactly when need_b − use_b > need_a − use_a. So sort by gap, largest first. To get the charge, walk from the last chore back to the first: before chore i you need at least need_i, and also enough to cover use_i plus what the rest requires.
steps: Sort the chores by need − use, largest first.
Set charge = 0 (what is needed after the last chore).
Walk the sorted list from the end to the start: charge = max(charge + use, need).
pitfalls: Sorting by need alone. In [[6, 8], [1, 7]] that gives 13 instead of 9.
Returning just the sum of use, or just the largest need. Both are lower bounds, not the answer.
Walking the sorted order forwards with the backward formula. The recurrence describes what is needed before a chore given what comes after it.

solutions.title: Try every order
solutions.idea: For each permutation, the charge needed is the largest of need_i plus everything used before chore i. Take the best order.

solutions.title: Sort by unused slack, then walk backwards
solutions.idea: Chores that leave the most charge unspent go first. The backward walk gives the exact charge for that order.

followups: Some chores give charge back instead of using it. How does the ordering rule change?
Prove the exchange argument: why does swapping two adjacent chores never touch the requirement of the others?
lcTitle: Minimum Initial Energy to Finish Tasks
